title: CS core facts
description: Operating systems, networks and databases answers that placement interviews keep asking for.

cards.back: Client sends SYN, server replies SYN-ACK, client sends ACK. Both sides now agree on initial sequence numbers and the connection is established.

cards.front: TCP vs UDP in one line each
cards.back: TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, with flow and congestion control. UDP: connectionless, no delivery or order guarantee, low overhead (DNS, video calls, games).

cards.front: What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?
cards.back: DNS lookup -> TCP connection (and TLS handshake for https) -> HTTP request -> server processes and responds -> browser parses HTML, fetches CSS/JS/images, builds the DOM and renders.

cards.front: ACID: {{c1::Atomicity}} (all or nothing), {{c2::Consistency}} (valid state to valid state), {{c3::Isolation}} (concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work), {{c4::Durability}} (committed data survives a crash).

cards.back: A process has its own address space and resources. Threads of one process share its memory and open files but have their own stack and registers. Thread switches are cheaper; a crashing thread can bring down the whole process.
Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one of them to prevent deadlock (for example, always lock in a fixed order to break circular wait).
A mutex is a lock owned by the thread that holds it (one at a time). A semaphore is a counter that allows up to N holders and can be signalled by a different thread.

cards.front: What is virtual memory and what is a page fault?
cards.back: Each process sees its own address space, mapped to physical frames in pages. A page fault happens when the page is not in RAM; the OS loads it from disk (or kills the process on an invalid access).
1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups. 2NF: 1NF and no partial dependency on part of a composite key. 3NF: 2NF and no transitive dependency (non-key columns depend only on the key).

cards.front: Why does an index speed up reads and what does it cost?
cards.back: A B-tree index finds rows in O(log n) instead of scanning the table. It costs disk space and makes inserts, updates and deletes slower because the index must be maintained.
INNER keeps only rows that match on both sides. LEFT keeps every row of the left table; where there is no match the right-side columns are NULL.
WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation (it can use COUNT, SUM and so on).

cards.front: The CAP theorem: during a network {{c1::partition}} a distributed store must choose between {{c2::consistency}} and {{c3::availability}}.
HTTP status classes and three to remember
cards.back: 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created), 3xx redirect (301, 302), 4xx client error (400, 401, 403, 404, 429), 5xx server error (500, 502, 503).
Stack: fast, per-thread, holds call frames and locals, freed automatically on return. Heap: shared, for objects that outlive a call, managed by hand (C/C++) or a garbage collector.
Encapsulation hides state behind a controlled interface (private fields, getters). Abstraction exposes only what a caller needs, hiding how it works (interfaces, abstract classes).
